blocks.title: Structural biology
blocks.text: Structural biology is the study of the three-dimensional (3D) structures of macromolecules, including proteins and nucleic acids, at the atomic level. It gives detailed information about the structure of a biomolecule, its functions, its dynamics, and its interaction with ligands and other macromolecules.
Structural biology has a wide range of applications, especially in medical research. Four are discussed here.

Structural biologists can determine the 3D structures of macromolecules such as proteins and nucleic acids. These structures reveal the exact location, shape and environment of the active sites and of the different domains, the distinct structural units with independent functions, of a macromolecule. For example, structural studies of the enzyme HIV-1 reverse transcriptase have identified its polymerase domain, which synthesises DNA, and its RNase H domain, which breaks down the RNA strand of RNA-DNA hybrids. Knowing the location and structure of these domains has helped in the design of antiviral drugs that specifically target them. Similarly, the structure of the serine proteases reveals a well-defined active site responsible for breaking peptide bonds.

blocks.alt: Two surface drawings of proteins. (a) HIV-1 reverse transcriptase: a large dark-blue body with light-green lobes and a nucleic-acid double helix lying across it; one circled lobe is the Polymerase domain and another the Nuclease domain. (b) Serine protease: a grey globular surface with a small cyan and red pocket circled and labelled Active site.
blocks.caption: Figure 7.1: (a) 3D structure of HIV-1 reverse transcriptase; (b) 3D structure of serine protease (original drawing after the textbook's Figure 7.1).

blocks.text: Structural biology helps scientists find the right place on a disease-causing molecule where a drug can work. These places are usually proteins and are called drug targets. By studying the 3D shape of these proteins, scientists find specific spots where a drug can attach and stop the protein from working. In COVID-19, scientists used structural biology to study the spike protein of the coronavirus SARS-CoV-2, which helps the virus enter human cells. Knowing its 3D structure, they identified it as a drug target and designed vaccines and medicines that block the spike protein, preventing the virus from infecting more cells.

Structural biology also helps in understanding how pathogens such as viruses and bacteria interact with the host's body cells, the host-pathogen interaction. By studying the 3D structures of both the pathogen's and the host cell's proteins, scientists can see how the pathogen attaches to and enters the host cell and which molecules are involved. Structural biologists studied the spike protein that sticks out from the surface of the coronavirus and also the protein on human cells that acts as the receptor for the spike, and so discovered exactly how the virus enters human cells. This information was vital in developing drugs that bind the receptor proteins; such a drug inhibits the interaction of the virus with the receptor and blocks the entry of the virus into the host cells.

blocks.alt: A human cell surface (blue) with two green Y-shaped ACE2 receptors. Above, a round SARS-CoV-2 particle covered with spike proteins binds one ACE2 receptor (SARS-CoV-2 spike protein binding to ACE2). Lower right, a second virus particle sits in a pocket of the membrane as it is taken into the cell (Viral entry, replication, and ACE2 normal function blocked).

blocks.text: The functionality of a protein depends on its correct folding into a three-dimensional shape. Several diseases, including cystic fibrosis, Parkinson's and Alzheimer's, originate from the incorrect folding of proteins. Structural biology provides an understanding of the intricate folding pathways and of how misfolding leads to these diseases.
